**Title**: How Does Schema Complexity Predict Performance in Training-Free LLM Information Extraction?

**Abstract**:
"""
Schema complexity affects training-free large language model (LLM) information extraction (IE), yet prior work conflates two factors: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability). We present, to our knowledge, the first controlled study isolating these factors in zero-shot LLM IE across four datasets, focusing on relation extraction (RE) as the primary testbed with named entity recognition (NER) and event detection as boundary conditions. Using embedding-based confusability metrics with controlled batch design, we find: (1) count degradation spans NER and RE (up to -49 percentage points [pp]), and inter-type confusability independently predicts RE type substitution errors, with bounded interaction confirmed by equivalence testing; (2) batch confusability independently explains ~27% of cross-batch RE accuracy variance on FewRel (semipartial R² = 0.273), replicating across two model families at three scales (8B-70B), while the NER null serves as a boundary condition; (3) schema decomposition fails due to merge amplification and routing failure, though oracle routing recovers accuracy.
